findings.explanation: event.sender is read without optional chaining. Messenger webhook events can arrive without a sender field (e.g. standby-channel events or a malformed/crafted payload), so this throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id'). The same file guards this exact field with ?. everywhere else it's touched (lines 286, 549, 552), showing the risk was known but this call site was missed. When handleEvent is invoked from processQueuedWebhookJob (line 620-643), a synchronous throw here happens before any catch for isNonRetryableMessengerSendError applies and gets rethrown at line 641, propagating into the queue consumer.

`body.entry || []` (and `entry.messaging || []` on the next line, 547) only guards against null/undefined — not against entry/messaging being a non-array (object, string, number). A crafted payload such as {"object":"page","entry":{}} makes `for...of` throw a TypeError synchronously, before res.sendStatus(200) is reached at line 572. Nothing in lines 531-579 wraps this in try/catch, so the async route handler's rejection is unhandled — the client never gets a response and the process is left with an unhandled promise rejection for a single crafted request.

inferBaseUrlFromRequest builds the base URL straight from the `x-forwarded-proto`/`x-forwarded-host` request headers (lines 290-291) with no allowlist or hostname validation. Unless a trusted proxy strictly overwrites these headers, they are attacker-controlled. This URL then flows into getMenuImageUrls/buildRequestedImageUrls (lines 971-974) to build image links that get sent to real customers over Messenger and fetched by Meta's servers — letting a forged header point those links at an attacker-controlled domain.
